bull.argument: Walmart's filing shows a business compounding at scale with improving fundamentals. Fiscal 2026 net sales rose 4.7% to $706.4 billion, operating income reached $29.8 billion, and consolidated net income grew to $22.3 billion from $20.2 billion. Walmart U.S. comparable sales rose 4.3%, with eCommerce contributing about 4.3 points, showing the omnichannel strategy is generating real growth rather than just spending. Free cash flow increased to $14.9 billion from $12.7 billion despite a $2.9 billion rise in capex, and the company approved a $30.0 billion buyback and raised its dividend to $0.99 per share. Returns remain high, with ROA at 8.2% and ROI at 15.1%. The filing does flag real risks, including the $0.9 billion rise in self-insured liability claims, a $0.7 billion PhonePe charge, and tariff uncertainty. Still, those headwinds were absorbed while operating income grew, and the company rates AA from S&P and Fitch.

claims.claim: Fiscal 2026 growth was broad, with net sales up 4.7% and net income rising to $22.3 billion.
claims.quote: Our total revenues increased $32.2 billion or 4.7% and $32.9 billion or 5.1% for fiscal 2026 and 2025

claims.claim: eCommerce is a clear contributor to Walmart U.S. comparable sales growth.
claims.quote: Walmart U.S. eCommerce sales positively contributed approximately 4.3% and 2.9% to comparable sales for fiscal 2026 and 2025

claims.claim: Free cash flow improved despite higher capital spending, and shareholder returns expanded.
claims.quote: Free cash flow for fiscal 2026 increased when compared to fiscal 2025 due to an increase in cash provided by operating income

bear.argument: The bull case rests on growth that is being bought with rising costs and capital. Capital expenditures climbed to $26.6 billion from $23.8 billion, and the filing says the increase supports omnichannel growth, yet free cash flow rose only $2.3 billion and remains thin relative to the $30.0 billion buyback authorization. Operating margin fell to 4.2% from 4.4%, and ROI declined to 15.1% from 15.5% as invested capital grew. Operating expenses rose to 20.9% of net sales from 20.7%, driven by a $0.9 billion increase in self-insured general liability claims and a $0.7 billion PhonePe charge. Net income was lifted by a $2.1 billion gain on equity investments, which the filing says fluctuates with stock prices, so it is not a clean measure of operating strength. The filing also warns that eCommerce growth could reduce in-store traffic, that AI investments may not deliver expected benefits, and that tariffs will continue into fiscal 2027 with an impact that 'could be material.' Short-term borrowings rose to $6.6 billion from $3.1 billion, and the working capital deficit widened to $22.6 billion.

claims.claim: Capital spending is rising faster than the free cash flow it produces, and returns on capital are declining.
claims.quote: ROI was 15.1% and 15.5% for fiscal 2026 and 2025, respectively. The decrease in ROI was primarily due to an increase in average invested capital

claims.claim: Net income was boosted by non-operating investment gains that the filing says can fluctuate, while operating margin declined.
claims.quote: Other gains and losses resulted in a net gain of $2.1 billion and a net loss of $0.8 billion in fiscal 2026 and 2025, respectively

claims.claim: Management warns that tariff impacts could be material and will continue into the next fiscal year.
claims.quote: We expect the dynamic tariff environment to continue, including in fiscal 2027, and cannot predict with certainty the future impact that this environment will have on our results of operations or financial performance, which could be material.

bull.argument: The bear case leans on real but mostly known trade-offs, and the filing shows them being absorbed. Operating income still grew to $29.8 billion from $29.3 billion, and the margin dip to 4.2% came mainly from the $0.9 billion self-insured claims increase and the $0.7 billion PhonePe charge, both disclosed one-time-style items rather than a broken core. Gross profit rate rose 8 basis points, and Walmart U.S. operating income rose $1.3 billion. Free cash flow grew to $14.9 billion even after $2.9 billion more capex, and the filing attributes part of that gain to lower cash taxes and payment timing, which the bear case omits. The $2.1 billion equity gain is a fair caveat, but it is excluded from operating income and was not needed to show operating growth. Higher short-term borrowings and a larger working capital deficit are normal for a company that runs with negative working capital and holds AA-rated long-term debt, with $15.0 billion of undrawn U.S. credit lines. Tariffs and AI risks are real, yet the filing says less than one third of U.S. sales are imported, and the $30.0 billion buyback is funded largely from free cash flow.

claims.claim: Operating income grew even as margin dipped, with the margin pressure tied to identified items.
claims.quote: Operating income $ 29,825 $ 29,348 Operating income as a percentage of net sales 4.2 % 4.4 %

claims.claim: The company funds its buyback largely from free cash flow and holds ample liquidity.
claims.quote: We anticipate that a majority of the ongoing share repurchase program will be funded through the Company's free cash flow.

claims.claim: Tariff exposure is bounded because less than one third of U.S. sales are imported.
claims.quote: less than one third of what we sell in the U.S. is imported, with most of our imports coming from China, Mexico, Vietnam, India and Canada

bear.argument: The opponent concedes the core trade-offs but explains them away. Operating income rose only $0.5 billion, from $29.3 billion to $29.8 billion, while net sales grew 4.7% and operating expenses rose faster as a share of sales. Margin fell 13 basis points. Calling the $0.9 billion claims increase and $0.7 billion PhonePe charge 'one-time-style' is a stretch: the filing describes rising self-insured claims costs 'across retail and related industries,' which is a trend, not a one-off. Free cash flow of $14.9 billion is partly flattered by lower cash taxes and payment timing, which the filing says may reverse in future periods. Capex is rising to a projected $25 to $27 billion in fiscal 2027, so the cash cushion is being consumed by investment. The $30.0 billion buyback is only partly covered: the filing says 'a majority' is funded from free cash flow, meaning the rest is not. Working capital deficit and short-term borrowings more than doubled in average terms, and the filing says tariffs 'could be material' next year.

claims.claim: Operating margin declined, and the cost pressures are described as a trend rather than one-time items.
claims.quote: higher self-insured general liability claims expense in the U.S. of approximately $0.9 billion, influenced by rising costs to resolve claims across retail and related industries

claims.claim: Free cash flow benefited from timing and lower cash taxes that the filing says may change in future periods.
claims.quote: Certain provisions decreased cash taxes paid in fiscal 2026 and may change the timing of cash tax payments in future periods.

claims.claim: The buyback is not fully covered by free cash flow, since the filing says only a majority is expected to be funded that way.
claims.quote: We anticipate that a majority of the ongoing share repurchase program will be funded through the Company's free cash flow.

judge.reasoning: Both sides cite verified quotes from the filing, so evidence is comparably strong. The bull effectively rebuts the bear's margin and equity-gain points by noting operating income grew and the gain is excluded from operating income, while the bear's strongest point (cost trends across the industry, cash tax timing, and the 'majority' funding language for the buyback) is partly answered but not fully countered. Neither side decisively wins, so this is close to even.
